english: as much as / to the same degree as (N)
formNote: Attach 만큼 directly to a noun with no spacing and no sound change (너 → 너만큼, 형 → 형만큼, 돈 → 돈만큼). It sets one thing as the yardstick: 'X is as Adj as N.' It also attaches to the modifier forms of verbs/adjectives (먹은 만큼 = as much as you ate, 노력한 만큼 = as much as you tried), but there 만큼 is spaced. As a particle on a plain noun it is the most common everyday use.
usage: I want to be as good as you
Noun as the standard of comparison
It's not as expensive as I thought
You get out as much as you put in
I ate as much as I wanted/could
먹을 만큼 = as much as one will eat
examples: 솔직히 월급만큼 일하면 됐죠 뭐.
Honestly, doing as much work as my salary is fine, right.
월급만큼 = as much as the paycheck; relatable work attitude
기대한 만큼 재미있진 않았어요.
It wasn't as fun as I'd hoped.
기대한 만큼 = as much as I expected; modifier form is spaced
한국어 진짜 너만큼만 했으면 좋겠다.
I really wish I were just as good at Korean as you.
너만큼만 adds 만 = 'just as much as you,' no more
mistakes: Spacing it off a plain noun: write 너만큼 (one word), not 너 만큼. After a verb/adjective modifier, though, it IS spaced: 한 만큼.

english: considering it's (an) N / for an N (it's surprisingly...)
formNote: Attach 치고 directly to a noun with no spacing (초보 → 초보치고, 겨울 → 겨울치고). It means 'given that it's N, it goes against what you'd expect from N.' You can add 는 → 치고는 to lean harder on the contrast. There's a second, opposite use, N치고 + negative = 'there's no N that isn't...' (한국 사람치고 김치 안 먹는 사람 없어요 = no Korean doesn't eat kimchi), so context tells the two apart.
usage: Standard 'better than expected for an N'
examples: 신상치고 가성비 괜찮은 편이에요.
For a new release, the value's pretty decent.
신상 = new product, 가성비 = bang for the buck; shopping talk
월요일치고는 도로가 안 막히네요.
For a Monday, the roads aren't that jammed.
치고는 leans into the surprise; commute small talk
걔 신입치고 일 진짜 잘해.
For a newbie, he's seriously good at the job.
신입 = new hire; casual workplace praise
mistakes: Spacing it: 초보 치고 is wrong — write 초보치고. Also don't confuse it with 치다 (to hit); here it's a particle of comparison.

english: looks / seems (a certain way) — judging by appearance
formNote: Take an adjective's -아/어 form and add 보이다 (spaced): stems with ㅏ/ㅗ take -아 보이다 (좋다 → 좋아 보이다, 작다 → 작아 보이다), others take -어 보이다 (어리다 → 어려 보이다, 힘들다 → 힘들어 보이다), and 하다 adjectives → 해 보이다 (피곤하다 → 피곤해 보이다). 예쁘다 drops ㅡ → 예뻐 보이다, 바쁘다 → 바빠 보이다. It's only for things you judge by looking; for guesses from other evidence use -(으)ㄴ/는 것 같다.
usage: You look like you're in a good mood
examples: 오늘따라 좀 안 좋아 보이는데 무슨 일 있어요?
You look a bit off today — is something wrong?
오늘따라 = today of all days; caring check-in
이 화장하니까 한 살은 어려 보인다.
With this makeup you look a year younger.
Casual beauty compliment; 어려 보이다 is the go-to phrase
그 패딩 따뜻해 보여서 샀어요.
I bought that puffer because it looked warm.
패딩 = puffer jacket; appearance-based reason
mistakes: Using it for non-visual guesses. 'It seems he's busy (from his texts)' is 바쁜 것 같아요, not 바빠 보여요 — 보이다 is for what you actually SEE.

formNote: Attach 에 비해 to a noun (작년 → 작년에 비해, 가격 → 가격에 비해). 비해 is the -아/어 form of 비하다 (to compare); you can also say the fuller 에 비해서 in speech or 에 비하여 in writing/formal speech. To compare against a verb/adjective clause, nominalize first: V-는 것에 비해 (사는 것에 비해 = compared to living...). It's the natural way to frame 'relative to N, this is more/less...'
usage: It's expensive compared to last year
가격에 비해 = relative to the price
You look young for your age
The result is poor relative to the effort
examples: 서울은 지방에 비해 월세가 훨씬 비싸요.
Rent in Seoul is way higher compared to outside the capital.
지방 = the provinces/non-capital; 월세 = monthly rent
연차에 비해 연봉이 좀 짠 편이에요.
For my years of experience, the salary's a bit stingy.
연차 = years on the job, 연봉 = annual salary; 짜다 = stingy
요즘 카페는 분위기에 비해 커피가 비싼 것 같아.
These days cafes feel pricey for the coffee relative to the vibe.
분위기 = atmosphere; common young-adult gripe
mistakes: Dropping 에: it's N에 비해, not N 비해. And don't write 비교해 here — the set phrase uses 비하다 → 비해.

english: even though / despite the fact that
formNote: It's the -는데/-(으)ㄴ데 background ending plus 도 (even). For present verbs use -는데도 (먹다 → 먹는데도, 하다 → 하는데도); for adjectives use -(으)ㄴ데도 (춥다 → 추운데도, 바쁘다 → 바쁜데도); for the past (both) use -았/었는데도 (잤는데도 = even though I slept). Nouns take N인데도. It sets up 'even given X, surprisingly Y' — stronger and more emotional than plain -지만.
usage: Even though I worked hard, I failed
Even though it's cold, I go out
Even though I ate, I'm hungry
Even though I'm broke, I bought it again
examples: 야근 많이 했는데도 월급은 그대로네요.
Even after all the overtime, my salary's the same.
야근 = overtime; resigned complaint
분명히 알람 맞춰 놨는데도 또 늦잠 잤어.
I clearly set an alarm and still overslept again.
늦잠 자다 = oversleep; everyday frustration
다이어트 하는데도 살이 안 빠져요.
Even though I'm dieting, I'm not losing weight.
살이 빠지다 = lose weight; very relatable
mistakes: Mixing the verb/adjective forms: present verbs take -는데도 (하는데도), adjectives take -(으)ㄴ데도 (추운데도). Saying 춥는데도 is wrong.

english: only / merely (do) — nothing more than that
formNote: Attach -ㄹ 뿐이다 to vowel-ending stems (하다 → 할 뿐이다) and -을 뿐이다 to consonant-ending stems (믿다 → 믿을 뿐이다); 뿐 is spaced from the modifier. For a past 'I only did,' use -았/었을 뿐이다 (도와줬을 뿐이에요 = I only helped). After a noun it becomes N일 뿐이다. It limits the situation to exactly one thing — 'that's all there is to it,' often defensively or modestly.
usage: Limiting your action to one thing
examples: 저는 그냥 시키는 대로 했을 뿐이에요.
I just did what I was told, that's all.
시키는 대로 = as told; deflecting blame at work
좋아하는 게 아니라 그냥 친한 동기일 뿐이야.
It's not that I like him, he's just a close peer.
동기 = same-cohort coworker/classmate; clearing up gossip
불평하는 게 아니라 사실을 말할 뿐이에요.
I'm not complaining, I'm only stating a fact.
Common way to soften a blunt remark
mistakes: Confusing it with 뿐만 아니라 (not only). -(으)ㄹ 뿐이다 closes things off ('only that'); 뿐만 아니라 opens them up ('and also').

formNote: Attach -ㄹ 뿐만 아니라 to vowel stems (싸다 → 쌀 뿐만 아니라) and -을 뿐만 아니라 to consonant stems (좋다 → 좋을 뿐만 아니라); for past actions use -았/었을 뿐만 아니라. The handiest form is the noun one, N뿐만 아니라 (돈뿐만 아니라 = not only money), where 뿐만 attaches straight to the noun. The second clause adds something further, usually with 도 (also): 'not only A, but B too.'
usage: It's not only tasty but also cheap
Not just me — everyone's like that
I not only work but also study
It's not only in Seoul but also in the provinces
examples: 이 집은 가성비 좋을 뿐만 아니라 사장님도 친절해요.
This place isn't just good value — the owner's friendly too.
가성비 = value for money; restaurant rec
걔는 일 잘할 뿐만 아니라 성격도 좋아서 인기 많아.
He's not only good at work but also nice, so he's popular.
성격 = personality; describing a coworker
요즘 물가는 월세뿐만 아니라 식비까지 다 올랐어요.
Lately prices have risen for not just rent but food too.
물가 = cost of living, 식비 = food expenses; noun form
mistakes: Spacing the noun form wrong: it's 돈뿐만 아니라 (뿐 attaches to the noun), with a space only before 아니라. Don't write 돈 뿐만.

english: in order to / for the sake of (doing)
formNote: Attach -기 위해(서) to a verb stem (모으다 → 모으기 위해, 합격하다 → 합격하기 위해); 위해서 (with 서) is common in speech, 위하여 is the formal/written form. After a noun, use N을/를 위해(서) (가족 → 가족을 위해 = for my family). It marks a deliberate goal, so it sounds a touch more formal/purposeful than the casual -(으)려고; great for written goals, resolutions, and explanations.
usage: I work part-time to save money
I study in order to pass
I skip meals to lose weight
examples: 전세금 모으기 위해서 진짜 안 쓰고 살고 있어요.
I'm living super frugally to save up for a jeonse deposit.
전세금 = lump-sum housing deposit; major young-adult goal
비자 연장하기 위해 출입국에 다녀왔어요.
I went to immigration to extend my visa.
출입국 = immigration office; practical for residents
더 나은 조건을 위해 이직 준비 중이에요.
I'm prepping a job change for better conditions.
이직 = changing jobs; noun + 위해
mistakes: Attaching it to a noun without 을/를: say 건강을 위해, not 건강 위해. For verbs it's the -기 form, not the dictionary form: 모으기 위해, not 모으다 위해.

english: as long as / so long as (a condition holds)
formNote: Attach -는 한 to a verb stem (살다 → 사는 한, with ㄹ dropping before ㄴ; 있다 → 있는 한). It very often appears in the negative, V-지 않는 한 (포기하지 않는 한 = as long as you don't give up), meaning 'unless.' 한 here means 'the limit/extent,' so the clause sets the boundary condition under which the main clause stays true. It's firmer and more conditional than a plain -(으)면 'if.'
usage: as long as you don't give up, it works
I'll help as much as I can
할 수 있는 한 = to the extent possible
I'll go as soon as possible
가능한 한 = as far as possible (set phrase)
examples: 계약서에 사인 안 하는 한 환불 돼요.
As long as you don't sign the contract, you can get a refund.
계약서 = contract; practical consumer point
여기 사는 한 그 정도 소음은 그냥 참아야 돼.
As long as you live here, you've gotta just put up with that much noise.
Casual roommate/neighbor reality
특별한 일 없는 한 보통 9시까지 출근해요.
Unless something special comes up, I usually get in by 9.
출근 = go to work; 없는 한 = unless there is
mistakes: Forgetting that 살다/알다 drop ㄹ before -는: it's 사는 한 / 아는 한, not 살는 한. Also don't read this 한 as the number 'one.'

english: so much that... / as a result of being so... (and then something happened)
formNote: Attach the past modifier -(으)ㄴ + 나머지 to verbs and adjectives (놀라다 → 놀란 나머지, 긴장하다 → 긴장한 나머지, 기쁘다 → 기쁜 나머지); consonant stems take -은 나머지 (참다 → 참은 나머지). It means an extreme degree of the first clause CAUSED the (usually negative or surprising) result in the second. It's a bit literary/dramatic, so it shines in storytelling, news, and vivid retellings rather than casual chit-chat.
usage: I was so startled that I screamed
I was so nervous I stammered
He was so angry he just left
I was so happy that I cried
examples: 너무 긴장한 나머지 면접에서 이름까지 까먹었어요.
I was so nervous I even forgot my name in the interview.
면접 = job interview; 까먹다 = forget; dramatic retelling
급한 나머지 지갑도 안 챙기고 나왔지 뭐야.
I was in such a rush I left without even my wallet.
급하다 = be in a hurry; casual storytelling with -지 뭐야
당황한 나머지 엉뚱한 버스를 타 버렸어요.
I was so flustered I ended up taking the wrong bus.
당황하다 = be flustered, 엉뚱한 = wrong/random; vivid mishap
mistakes: Using the present -는 나머지 — this pattern takes the past modifier -(으)ㄴ: 놀란 나머지, not 놀라는 나머지.
